newsitem.title: USA: Holiday shopping off to an early start.
newsitem.headline: Holiday shopping off to an early start.

text.p: The shorter holiday shopping season has Americans flocking to malls earlier this year, much to the delight of retailers, industry officials and analysts said.

"If I have fewer shopping days, I don't cut out one of the kids from the shopping list," said Dan Seto, a senior economist with Nikko Securities. "The money will be spent whether we have the days or not."

This year there are 26 days between Thanksgiving and Christmas, while last year there were 31. Hanukkah is earlier this year than last, which analysts said should also give holiday spending an early boost.

Sears, Roebuck and Co. Chairman Arthur Martinez expects December sales to rise about 6 percent from last year on a store-for-store basis, after healthy weekend business indicated the holiday season got off to a strong start.

"We feel good about the prospects for the season," Martinez said in an interview on Monday. "Judging off this weekend's business -- the kind of traffic and activity I saw this weekend -- customers are ready to do business."
Analysts said sales lagged last year, unnerving retailers and driving heavy promotions and deep markdowns early in the season. That was not expected to be the case this year.
"People will get out there, do shopping early, (retailers) won't panic and gross margins will be strong for retailers across the board," said David Lebedeff, an analyst at NatCity Investments.

Industry indicators have generally pointed to an increase of about 5 percent in holiday sales compared with last year, as employment remains strong and salaries are rising while inflation remains in check.
A survey released on Monday by the Conference Board, a business research group, said retail sales would rise 5.5 percent over last year's holiday season sales, topping the $45 billion mark.

The study found the average American household will spend $450 on gifts -- up from $430 in 1995. New England was seen leading the way with purchases expected to average $722 per household, the report said.
Redbook Research, a unit of Lynch, Jones & Ryan Inc., has also projected a 5 percent to 5.5 percent increase in sales. The firm surveys major retailers each week.
"Most are saying sales are up to expectations for the month of November," said Howard Eilenberg an analyst at Redbook. "If that continues I think certainly the 5.5 percent figure is achievable."
In another report released Tuesday, the Conference Board said consumer confidence was strong.

"This strong level of confidence, coupled with low unemployment, modest inflationary pressures and continuing wage growth, should translate into healthy holiday sales in coming weeks," the group said.
Analysts said they expected department store sales and clothing sales to shine this year in comparison with dismal results last year.

"I think it really has more to do with the replenishment cycle of a wardrobe, and the fact that people aren't spending in other categories," said Dean Ramos, vice president and retail analyst for Dain Bosworth.
In addition to Sears, Dayton Hudson Corp. and women's apparel chains AnnTaylor Stores Corp. and The Limited Inc. all reported higher third-quarter sales, pointing to a rosy holiday season.
"While the holiday calendar is challenging, we believe we are well positioned for a successful finish to 1996," Dayton Hudson Chairman Bob Ulrich said in a statement.

But while clothing and home furnishings sales at stores such as Crate & Barrel and Williams Sonoma are strong, computer retailers are finding it hard to live up to last year's stellar performance, which was boosted by the launch of Microsoft's Windows 95 operating system.
Electronics retailer Best Buy Co. Inc., for example, said earlier this month it expects to report third-quarter profits "significantly below" year-ago levels.

"There is concern that people don't want to take on a lot more debt, but it's easy to buy a shirt or a dress," Redbook's Eilenberg said. "There's no single thing like Windows 95 this year to give that market a real push."
